justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift across the three horizons, anchored around a current price or index level near 55.7. At the one-day horizon, the estimate stays close to the prevailing level because short-term price dynamics tend to be mean-reverting in the absence of major scheduled catalysts, and any overnight information has likely already been partially absorbed. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 56.0, reflecting a modest positive drift assumption consistent with a slight bullish bias in underlying fundamentals or recent momentum. The one-month estimate of 56.5 extends that drift further, incorporating a longer runway for any structural tailwinds to materialize, though the increment remains modest because compounding uncertainty over that horizon limits my confidence in directional calls.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the classic square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty in financial or probabilistic forecasting. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 1.5 units on each side, consistent with typical daily volatility being relatively contained. By one week, the interval expands to roughly ±3.2 units, capturing the possibility of several consecutive adverse or favorable sessions. At one month, the interval stretches to ±6 units, acknowledging that over four weeks, macroeconomic data releases, policy decisions, geopolitical developments, and sentiment shifts can collectively move prices well beyond what short-term volatility alone would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected policy tightening announcement, a deterioration in key economic indicators, or a sudden liquidity event could cause a sharp move well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where the market would have more time to reprice. On the upside, a positive surprise in earnings, economic data, or geopolitical resolution could drive a rally that exceeds the upper bound, especially at the one-month horizon where positive catalysts have more time to compound.

It is also worth acknowledging model risk as a source of tail exposure. My intervals assume a roughly symmetric, relatively well-behaved distribution of outcomes, but financial variables often exhibit fat tails and skewness. A genuine regime change — such as a sudden shift in monetary policy stance or an exogenous shock — could render the entire distribution stale, pushing realized outcomes far outside what any reasonable confidence interval would have captured at the time of the forecast. These tail events are by definition low-probability but are precisely the scenarios that interval forecasts tend to underweight.
